title: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry

cards.explanation: The lecture distinguishes sequence, length and structural variation; categories can overlap.
cards.text: A difference in DNA base identity is a {{c1::sequence polymorphism}}.
cards.question: A difference in DNA base identity is a {{c1::sequence polymorphism}}.

cards.explanation: It denotes a single nucleotide polymorphism; not every variant is pathogenic.
cards.text: The most common single-base marker category is a {{c1::SNP}}.
cards.question: The most common single-base marker category is a {{c1::SNP}}.

cards.explanation: Non-coding does not automatically mean functionless or without a disease association.
cards.text: Many SNPs occur in {{c1::non-coding sequence}}.
cards.question: Many SNPs occur in {{c1::non-coding sequence}}.

cards.explanation: They help distinguish genomic regions and follow inheritance.
cards.text: Stable inherited SNPs can act as genetic {{c1::markers}}.
cards.question: Stable inherited SNPs can act as genetic {{c1::markers}}.

cards.explanation: Interspersed repeats occur at separated positions instead.
cards.text: Adjacent copies of a repeated DNA motif form a {{c1::tandem repeat}}.
cards.question: Adjacent copies of a repeated DNA motif form a {{c1::tandem repeat}}.

cards.explanation: The motif can remain the same while array length changes.
cards.text: Variation in the number of tandem repeat copies creates a {{c1::length polymorphism}}.
cards.question: Variation in the number of tandem repeat copies creates a {{c1::length polymorphism}}.

cards.explanation: Misalignment during replication can add or remove repeated units.
cards.text: DNA-polymerase slippage can change the {{c1::repeat number}}.
cards.question: DNA-polymerase slippage can change the {{c1::repeat number}}.

cards.explanation: One product can gain material while another loses it.
cards.text: Misaligned recombination between repeats can cause {{c1::unequal crossing over}}.
cards.question: Misaligned recombination between repeats can cause {{c1::unequal crossing over}}.

cards.explanation: AAAA is a four-copy array of a one-base motif.
cards.text: A repeated tract of a single nucleotide is a {{c1::homopolymer}}.
cards.question: A repeated tract of a single nucleotide is a {{c1::homopolymer}}.

cards.explanation: Distinguish number of repeats from total length, which is eight bases.
cards.text: The sequence ATATATAT contains {{c1::four}} copies of the AT motif.
cards.question: The sequence ATATATAT contains {{c1::four}} copies of the AT motif.

cards.explanation: GCG is repeated five times; total array length is fifteen bases.
cards.text: The repeat-unit size of GCGGCGGCGGCGGCG is {{c1::three bases}}.
cards.question: The repeat-unit size of GCGGCGGCGGCGGCG is {{c1::three bases}}.

cards.explanation: Definitions vary among sources; this is the range used in these lecture slides.
cards.text: The lecture calls short 2–10-base tandem-repeat motifs {{c1::microsatellites}}.
cards.question: The lecture calls short 2–10-base tandem-repeat motifs {{c1::microsatellites}}.

cards.explanation: The unit size and array length are different measurements.
cards.text: A whole DNA segment composed of repeated motifs is a repeat {{c1::array}}.
cards.question: A whole DNA segment composed of repeated motifs is a repeat {{c1::array}}.

cards.explanation: Repeat-category boundaries vary among references.
cards.text: In the lecture's classification, 11–100-base repeat units are {{c1::minisatellites}}.
cards.question: In the lecture's classification, 11–100-base repeat units are {{c1::minisatellites}}.

cards.explanation: STR usually refers specifically to short tandem repeats; the slide's broad grouping should not make all repeat types identical.
cards.text: VNTR expands to variable number {{c1::tandem repeat}}.
cards.question: VNTR expands to variable number {{c1::tandem repeat}}.

cards.explanation: The source also calls it a mobile genetic element.
cards.text: A DNA element capable of changing genomic position is a {{c1::transposon}}.
cards.question: A DNA element capable of changing genomic position is a {{c1::transposon}}.

cards.explanation: LINE is the corresponding long interspersed nuclear-element category.
cards.text: SINE stands for short interspersed {{c1::nuclear element}}.
cards.question: SINE stands for short interspersed {{c1::nuclear element}}.

cards.explanation: The presence of a transposon-derived repeat does not mean it still jumps.
cards.text: Most transposon-derived sequences in humans are no longer {{c1::actively mobile}}.
cards.question: Most transposon-derived sequences in humans are no longer {{c1::actively mobile}}.

cards.explanation: An inversion alone changes orientation, not copy number; the source's list of rearrangements is broader than CNVs.
cards.text: A gain or loss that changes the number of copies of a DNA segment is {{c1::copy-number variation}}.
cards.question: A gain or loss that changes the number of copies of a DNA segment is {{c1::copy-number variation}}.

cards.explanation: Do not equate every structural variant with a duplication or deletion.
cards.text: A balanced inversion can be copy-number {{c1::neutral}}.
cards.question: A balanced inversion can be copy-number {{c1::neutral}}.

cards.explanation: They range in scale and can affect sequence, length and structure.
cards.text: The combined term for insertions and deletions is {{c1::indels}}.
cards.question: The combined term for insertions and deletions is {{c1::indels}}.

cards.explanation: It also supports ancestry and disease-susceptibility research.
cards.text: Normal genetic variation enables human identification and {{c1::kinship testing}}.
cards.question: Normal genetic variation enables human identification and {{c1::kinship testing}}.

cards.explanation: It also asks how frequencies change over time.
cards.text: Population genetics studies variation within and {{c1::between populations}}.
cards.question: Population genetics studies variation within and {{c1::between populations}}.

cards.explanation: Geography can help define a sampled population, but boundaries depend on the research question.
cards.text: A biological population contains members of the same species capable of {{c1::interbreeding}}.
cards.question: A biological population contains members of the same species capable of {{c1::interbreeding}}.

cards.explanation: Linked regions can nevertheless remain inherited together for many generations.
cards.text: Meiotic recombination produces chromosomes containing a {{c1::mixture of parental segments}}.
cards.question: Meiotic recombination produces chromosomes containing a {{c1::mixture of parental segments}}.

cards.explanation: It is a population-level association, not simply the physical fact that loci lie on one chromosome.
cards.text: Non-random association of alleles at different loci is {{c1::linkage disequilibrium}}.
cards.question: Non-random association of alleles at different loci is {{c1::linkage disequilibrium}}.

cards.explanation: Informative markers can label a larger inherited DNA segment.
cards.text: A set of variants carried together on one chromosome segment is a {{c1::haplotype}}.
cards.question: A set of variants carried together on one chromosome segment is a {{c1::haplotype}}.

cards.explanation: This avoids reading every base when tracking that segment.
cards.text: Markers within a haplotype can serve as a shortcut for a larger {{c1::DNA segment}}.
cards.question: Markers within a haplotype can serve as a shortcut for a larger {{c1::DNA segment}}.

cards.explanation: Haplogroups are useful for tracking particular lineages, not a complete summary of a person's ancestry.
cards.text: Related haplotypes can be grouped into a {{c1::haplogroup}}.
cards.question: Related haplotypes can be grouped into a {{c1::haplogroup}}.

cards.explanation: It reflects one inheritance route rather than all ancestors.
cards.text: Mitochondrial DNA usually tracks the {{c1::maternal lineage}}.
cards.question: Mitochondrial DNA usually tracks the {{c1::maternal lineage}}.

cards.explanation: This applies where a Y lineage is inherited and excludes recombining portions.
cards.text: The non-recombining Y region tracks the {{c1::paternal lineage}}.
cards.question: The non-recombining Y region tracks the {{c1::paternal lineage}}.

cards.explanation: She is not necessarily the most recent genealogical ancestor of all living humans.
cards.text: Mitochondrial Eve is a most recent shared ancestor for the {{c1::mitochondrial lineage}}.
cards.question: Mitochondrial Eve is a most recent shared ancestor for the {{c1::mitochondrial lineage}}.

cards.explanation: Other lineages can be lost over generations while descendants persist through other ancestry paths.
cards.text: Mitochondrial Eve was not the {{c1::only woman alive}} at her time.
cards.question: Mitochondrial Eve was not the {{c1::only woman alive}} at her time.

cards.explanation: They describe separate lineage-coalescence histories.
cards.text: Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosome Adam need not have lived {{c1::at the same time}}.
cards.question: Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosome Adam need not have lived {{c1::at the same time}}.

cards.explanation: It is not one fixed founding person independent of which present-day lineages remain.
cards.text: The identity of a lineage's most recent common ancestor can change as lineages {{c1::become extinct}}.
cards.question: The identity of a lineage's most recent common ancestor can change as lineages {{c1::become extinct}}.

cards.explanation: They provide small pieces of a broader genomic history.
cards.text: Maternal and paternal lineage tests omit most {{c1::autosomal ancestry}}.
cards.question: Maternal and paternal lineage tests omit most {{c1::autosomal ancestry}}.

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 2
slides.text:
L E A R N I N G  O B J E C T I V E S
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:
• List the different types of normal variation that occur between human 
genomes
• Provide examples of sequence, length, and structural polymorphisms
• Explain why normal genetic variation is a useful research tool in human 
genetics
• Describe the tracking of genetic fragments through linkage disequilibrium, 
haplotypes, and haplogroups

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 3
slides.text: W H E R E  A R E  W E ? ?

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 4
slides.text:
H O W  D O  H U M A N  G E N O M E S  D I F F E R ?
Similar but different
We know that any two randomly 
selected humans share ~99% of 
their DNA sequence and structure
Put differently, the sequence and 
structure of your own genome is 
about 99% similar to the 
reference human genome
What sorts of differences make 
up the remaining percentage?

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 5
slides.text:
H O W  D O  H U M A N  G E N O M E S  D I F F E R ?
Pathogenic vs polymorphic
Variation between genomes ranges 
from single nucleotide differences 
to gains and losses of whole 
chromosomes
Normal, polymorphic variation is 
limited to:
Sequence polymorphisms
Length polymorphisms
Structural polymorphisms
(Epigenetic differences)

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 6
slides.text:
S E Q U E N C E  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Snip snip….
The most common type of 
sequence polymorphism is a single 
nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
SNPs generally arise as single 
nucleotide replication errors 
passed down for several 
generations
A SNP occurs once in every 100-
300 bases
Each of us has about 11 million 
SNPs in our genome

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 7
slides.text:
S E Q U E N C E  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Cataloguing SNPs
More than 100+ million SNPs 
are known
Most SNPs occur in non-coding 
sequence
SNPs are stable differences 
between genomes, making them 
useful tools for examining 
different genomes

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 8
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
How long is a piece of DNA?
Length polymorphisms involve changes in 
frequency of a repeat unit
Over 50% of the genome is repetitive 
sequence
Repeated DNA sequences either occur in 
tandem (next door to each other) or are 
interspersed
Length polymorphisms refer mainly to 
tandem repeats

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 9
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Why why so so repetitive?
Replication of DNA is error prone
DNA polymerases can lose track of 
how many repeats have been 
replicated and how many await 
replication
When polymerase slips backward, 
new repeats are added (insertion). 
When polymerase slips forwards, 
some repeats are left out (deletion)

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 10
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
An unfair exchange
Aligning and recombining 
DNA is also error prone
Misaligned repeats can 
either cause unequal 
sister chromatid 
exchange (between 
strands of replicated 
DNA) or unequal 
crossover (between 
replicated chromosomes

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 11
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Size matters
The size of the repeated 
DNA sequence unit can 
range from 1 nucleotide, to 
over 1 million nucleotides!
Size ranges are given 
different names to help 
distinguish them

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 12
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Homopolymer
A homopolymer, or a 
homopolymer tract, is a 1 
nucleotide repeat unit
AAAA
GGGGGGG
TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT
Number of repeats: 4
Repeat unit size: 1 base
Number of repeats: 7
Number of repeats: 20

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 13
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Microsatellites
A microsatellite is a repeat 
unit consisting of 2-10 
bases
ATATATAT
GCGGCGGCGGCGGCG
Repeat unit size: 2 bases
Repeat unit size: 3 bases
Number of repeats: 4
Number of repeats: 5

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 14
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Other satellites
Minisatellites have a repeat 
unit of 11-100 bases
Satellites have a repeat unit 
of  ~100-400 bases
The entire segment of DNA 
consisting of a repeat motif 
is referred to as an array

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 15
slides.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
More terminology
Some arrays are fixed in size and don’t vary 
from one person to the next
However, most homopolymers, 
microsatellite, minisatellite, and  satellite 
arrays vary in size and are collectively 
referred to as variable number tandem 
repeats (VNTRs) or short tandem repeats 
(STRs)
VNTRs/STRs are the typical example of 
length polymorphisms

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 16
slides.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
An a-maize-ing discovery
Repeat units can also be interspersed 
throughout the genome, rather than occurring 
in tandem
Most of these interspersed repeats are 
transposons
A transposon is a DNA segment that can 
change its position in the genome (also known 
as a jumping gene or a mobile genetic element)

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 17
slides.text: S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 18
slides.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Signs and lines
There are two main families of transposons
Short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs)
Long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs)

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 19
slides.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Littered lines
Transposable elements are scattered throughout your entire 
genome, even between exons!
Most transposons in the human genome no longer “jump”

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 20
slides.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Do you copy?
Any repeat unit (whether tandem or 
interspersed) larger than 50 bases 
that shows variation between 
individuals is also known as a copy 
number variant (CNV)
Changes in the copy number of 
CNVs occur as the result of 
structural changes (insertion, 
deletion, translocation, duplication, 
inversion), and can thus be referred 
to as structural polymorphisms

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 21
slides.text: S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 22
slides.text:
P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
The special case of indels
Insertions and deletions (indels) of non-repeat motif DNA sequence sit at the 
intersection between sequence, length, and structural polymorphisms.
Indels can range in size from 1 base to entire chromosome segments
These can affect the sequence, length, and structure of the DNA

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 23
slides.text: N O R M A L  V A R I A T I O N

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 24
slides.text:
N O R M A L  V A R I A T I O N
Unique, just like 
everyone else
Understanding the ways in 
which genomes differ 
normally can be used to 
our advantage
Human identification
Paternity and kinship 
testing
Human history and 
evolution
Disease susceptibility

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 25
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Keeping track of what’s normal
Population genetics is the study of genetic variation within and between 
populations, and how this variation is maintained or changed over time.

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 26
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
What is a population?
A biological population is any group of members of the same species, living in the same 
geographical region, that interbreed or can potentially interbreed
To study genetic variation within a population, we need to count the amount of normal 
variation and determine how much this changes from one generation to the next
To do this, we first need to recall how genetic material is inherited

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 27
slides.text:
T H E  P R O C E S S  O F  I N H E R I T A N C E
Taking chunks from the gene pool
DNA is inherited in “chunks” 
Homologous chromosomes undergo recombination, so that the offspring receives 
a mixture of genetic material

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 28
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
A family affair
The global population is one large 
family
A chunk of DNA that is inherited as a 
unit (more commonly than statistics 
would predict) is known as a linkage 
disequilibrium block
Linkage – the DNA sequence is linked 
together to form a unit
Disequilibrium – the chunk of DNA is 
passed on as a whole unit more often 
than statistics would predict

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 29
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Chunk tracking
Because DNA is inherited in chunks that can stay intact for many generations, we can often identify 
chunks by just examining the normal variants on each chunk, instead of having to read the whole 
sequence
Since SNPs are so common in the human genome (1 every 100-300 bases), we can take note of which 
groups of SNPs seem to be inherited together more often than you would expect
This group of SNPs is called a haplotype -  a set of closely linked markers that are inherited together

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 30
slides.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 31
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Short hand
Haplotypes are a “shortcut” for 
referring to a much larger chunk of 
DNA
Similar haplotypes can be grouped 
together into “haplogroups”
When studying populations, we 
determine the frequency of normal 
variants, haplotypes, and/or 
haplogroups. This can be done in 
autosomes, sex chromosomes, or 
the mitochondrial genome

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 32
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Uniparental inheritance
Tracking haplotypes and haplogroups in the mitochondrial genome and the non-
recombining portion of the Y chromosome is how ancestry testing is done for 
your maternal and paternal heritage respectively.

slides.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

slides.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 35
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Adam and Eve
Theoretically, we could track the mitochondrial lineage of all extant humans back 
to one woman (mitochondrial Eve) and the non-recombining portion of the Y 
chromosome to one man (Y-chromosome Adam)

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 36
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
A more complicated story
Common misconceptions about mt-Eve 
and Y-MRCA reveal how challenging it is 
to conceptualise and track human 
history:
Not the only man/woman alive at the 
time
Not one fixed individual
Not alive at the same time as each other
Not the most recent common ancestor 
shared by all humans

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 37
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
One small piece of a much larger puzzle
Tracking only patrilineal and matrilineal heritage excludes the majority of the 
human genome
Population genetics must also have methods for tracking autosomal variation…but 
how?

slides.topic: Population Genetics I — Normal Variation, Haplotypes & Ancestry — source 38
slides.text:
S U M M A R Y
• Normal variation in the human genome can be loosely 
categorised into sequence, length, and structural 
polymorphisms
• Identifying and cataloguing normal variation between 
humans provides a useful tool for several different functions
• Population genetics is the discipline concerned with studying 
normal genetic variation and how it is maintained or 
changed over time
• It is easiest to track variation in non-recombining portions of 
the genome, but this has limited scope
